name: fast-pako (@r1ck404/fast-pako)
workload: gzip/inflate/deflate calls on real inputs (npm tarballs of typescript, react-dom, three; 1 MB and 9 MB JavaScript; tiny 75 B to 1 KB inputs), best of 3 rounds with each implementation in fresh processes
claimed_speedup: ungzip of 4.4 MB typescript tarball 99.8 ms vs 17.3 ms (5.8x); inflate 1 MB JS 3.18 vs 0.76 ms (4.2x); deflateRaw level 1 3.0x; deflate level 6 on 1 MB 2.1x; deflate level 6 on 75 B 20x; gzip 300 B 6.5x; first ungzip of a 1.4 MB tarball including import 49.7 vs 12.2 ms
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, no_std, explicit SIMD128, then binaryen wasm-opt (packages/fast-pako/rust/Cargo.toml and build.mjs); Node 24.16 and Chromium 149
stars_or_usage: 1 star (new, Sep-Oct 2026); published to npm as @r1ck404/fast-pako
tradeoffs: Needs WebAssembly (throws a clear error without it); bundle is slightly smaller than pako for the JS but gzip size doubles (30.6 KB vs 15.1 KB gzipped) because compiled wasm compresses worse; pako lib/* and dist/* subpaths are not provided; output is byte-identical to pako and the repo ships large differential test suites (7,864 equivalence checks plus fuzzers).
caveats: Single-maintainer repo with 37 commits and 1 star, written to speed up the Nodepod browser runtime; first-party benchmark, though the benchmark code (bench/) and raw results (results/) are public. Baseline is pako, a JS port of zlib, not native zlib or libdeflate. Small-input gains partly reflect pako's per-call setup cost. Raw timing tables are in the README; the page named in benchmark_url is the repo README.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' (registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search) surfaced @r1ck404/fast-pako, then the GitHub README of R1ck404/fast-packages

name: fast-noble-hashes (@r1ck404/fast-noble-hashes)
workload: one-shot and incremental sha512, sha384, sha256, sha1, md5, hmac, pbkdf2 and scrypt calls on real inputs (npm tarballs, 1 MB buffers, 56-character strings), best of 3 rounds in fresh processes
claimed_speedup: sha512 of 4.4 MB typescript tarball 30.47 ms vs 5.68 ms (5.4x Node, 6.0x Chromium); md5 1 MB 8.95 vs 1.15 ms (7.8x); sha1 1 MB 2.6x; sha256 1 MB 3.65 vs 2.12 ms (1.7x); pbkdf2(sha512) c=10000 7.2x; pbkdf2(sha256) 3.4x; scrypt N=2^14 2.3x; hmac(sha256) short key 1.3x; sha256.create() with 100 B updates 1.2x
compiler_and_flags: wasm kernels written as templates by a build-time assembler (wasm/kernels.mjs, wasm/asm.mjs) and scrypt in wasm/scrypt.wat, assembled and optimised with binaryen; requires WebAssembly SIMD; Node 24.16 and Chromium 149
stars_or_usage: 1 star (new, Sep-Oct 2026); published to npm as @r1ck404/fast-noble-hashes
tradeoffs: Must be installed under the name @noble/hashes (its utils import @noble/hashes/crypto by name); needs WebAssembly with SIMD (Node 16.4+, Chrome/Edge 91+, Firefox 89+); each hash family compiles its wasm on first use (about 1 ms, first sha256 call 1.2 ms vs 0.3 ms); bundle for sha256 alone grows from 4.7 KB to 7.6 KB; noble's non-accelerated hashes stay in JS.
caveats: Single-maintainer first-party benchmark (bench/ and results/ are public) in a repo with 37 commits; gains for sha256 are modest (1.2-2.4x) and small updates are close to parity. @noble/hashes is itself an audited constant-time-oriented library, and the wasm path trades that audit for speed; no independent review of the wasm kernels. Shares one repo with the fast-pako entry (distinguished here by the package subpath).
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript', then the GitHub README of R1ck404/fast-packages (noble-hashes section)

name: dhi (Zig SIMD WASM Zod 4 replacement)
language: Zig (compiled to SIMD WebAssembly, plus an N-API addon and a Python C extension)
workload: 25 schema-validation micro-benchmarks (string formats such as email/uuid/url/ipv4, number formats, ISO dates, coercion, objects, arrays, unions) comparing the dhi z.* drop-in API with Zod 4, run with Bun
claimed_speedup: README: 13.8x faster than Zod 4 on the full suite; number formats 30-50x, coercion 23-56x, string formats 12-27x, objects 4-7x, arrays 8x; URL validator 8.0x and IPv4 1.1x vs Zod in 1.3.1. benchmark-results.json (2026-03-18, runtime Bun): z.email() 6,608,838 vs 416,360 ops/s (15.9x), z.int() 54.3x, z.coerce.boolean() 74.5x, Object (valid) 4.4x, Array<number> 7.8x, Union 1.6x, Optional 2.2x
compiler_and_flags: zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast for the Zig core; TypeScript benchmark run as 'bun run benchmarks/benchmark-vs-all.ts'; Zod version not stated
tradeoffs: Browser and edge runtimes load a 28 KB SIMD WASM module; Node uses an N-API native addon (platform binaries); Zod 4 API parity is claimed but not complete for every refinement; Python side is a separate Pydantic replacement.
caveats: First-party; benchmark scripts are public but the CPU, Bun version and Zod version are not stated. The benchmark runs on Bun (JavaScriptCore), not V8, so it is not a measurement of Zod in V8. README speedups (13.8x suite, URL 8.0x, IPv4 1.1x) differ from the older benchmark-results.json (average 27.3x, URL 13.8x, IPv4 12.2x); the README chart is a PNG. Union and discriminated-union rows are only 1.6-2.1x. On Node the fast path is the native addon rather than WASM.
found_via: npm registry search 'webassembly simd fast' (dhi: 'Ultra-fast Zod 4 drop-in replacement - 20x faster average, full API parity, SIMD WASM'), then the GitHub README and docs/benchmarks/benchmark-results.json

name: @gmod/inflate (wasm libdeflate batch inflate)
language: Rust (libdeflater compiled to WebAssembly) with TypeScript
workload: Inflate of the real zlib blocks of four BigWig fixtures (49 to 489 blocks per file), whole block run per call, timed in Node against pako and the platform DecompressionStream; the wasm module was extracted from the bbi-js genome-file parser
claimed_speedup: README: inflateRawBatch is roughly 4x faster than pako on genomics block sizes. bbi-js docs/wasm.md: wasm 1.9 ms vs pako 6.0 ms on volvox.bw (49 blocks), 5.4 vs 16.6 ms on cow.bw (125), 31 vs 86 ms on ENCFF826FLP.bw (436), 29 vs 62 ms on variable_step_large.bw (489), i.e. 2.1-3.1x (derived from page data); the doc itself states 2.5-3x and says DecompressionStream is 4-11x slower than the wasm path
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate built to wasm (libdeflater), inlined as base64; release flags not stated; Node, version not stated
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (extracted August 2026 from bbi-js, 9 stars, 567 commits, used in GMOD genome-browser parsers)
tradeoffs: Decompression only (inflateRaw and inflateRawBatch), no compression; wasm inlined as base64 in one bundle (about 65 KB) and instantiated lazily; the speedup depends on batching many blocks in one JS-wasm crossing.
caveats: Benchmark code (benchmarks/inflate.bench.ts in bbi-js) is public but CPU, Node version and Rust flags are not stated, and the doc says ranges are across three runs on one machine and 'treat them as an order of magnitude'. The doc warns the 2.5-3x is inflate in isolation: an end-to-end whole-genome parseBigWig comparison was only about 5% apart. The README's '4x' is not backed by a table in inflate-js itself; the table with numbers lives in the sibling bbi-js repo (MIT, same author).
found_via: npm registry search 'keywords:wasm fast' (@gmod/inflate: 'Fast DEFLATE decompression via wasm libdeflate'), then the GitHub README and GMOD/bbi-js docs/wasm.md

name: calaminejs (calamine spreadsheet reader in WebAssembly)
language: Rust (calamine compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack) with TypeScript
baseline: SheetJS xlsx 0.18.5 (pure JavaScript spreadsheet parser in V8)
workload: Reading one large .xlsx sheet (1.8M cells, 23 MB) and medium (400k cells) and small (5k cells) sheets to CSV or cell arrays, median of N runs on Node 22.18
claimed_speedup: large sheet toCsv 865 ms vs SheetJS sheet_to_csv 4.57 s (5.3x); readCells values 981 ms vs sheet_to_json 4.61 s (4.7x); readCells tagged 1.53 s (3.0x); medium 400k cells 188 ms vs 786 ms (4.2x, derived from page data); small 5k cells 2 ms vs 8 ms (4x, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack (bun run build); release flags not stated; Node 22.18 (Bun 1.3.5 also run); comparison script bench/compare/run.mjs
tradeoffs: Read-only (no writing, styling or formula evaluation); no CSV input; 370 KB gzipped (720 KB raw) wasm artifact; the JS-wasm boundary adds 35-55% on top of the 634 ms parse for the large file; async wasm load needed in browsers (await ready()).
caveats: Author-run benchmark (the bench/ scripts and large fixtures are public, the CPU model is not stated). The README says 'up to 5x' while the tables show 3.0-5.3x on the large file and the docs/comparison.md section is candid that SheetJS has wider format coverage and maturity. SheetJS comparison uses the npm-latest 0.18.5 build. Unofficial binding of tafia/calamine, so the parsing speed is calamine's; repo is 27 commits old.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' (calamine: 'Fast xlsx/xls/xlsb/ods reader — calamine compiled to WebAssembly'), then the GitHub README and docs/comparison.md

name: ultrachess (Rust chess library compiled to WebAssembly)
baseline: chess.js (pure JavaScript chess library in V8/Node)
workload: Startpos perft depth 6 (119,060,324 nodes) through the WASM boundary via Chess.create() and chess.perft(6), plus geomean over six standard perft positions
claimed_speedup: WASM startpos d6 on Node 25.7.0: 353.7 ms, 336.7 Mnps; on Bun 1.3.10: 204.9 ms, 581.0 Mnps. chess.js is listed at 5-7 Mnps (cited from upstream, Node 22), so the README claims about 55x chess.js on Node and about 95x on Bun (about 48-67x on Node and 83-116x on Bun if computed from the 5-7 Mnps range, derived from page data); native Rust is about 140x chess.js
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.95.0, cargo --release with LTO fat and codegen-units 1, no SIMD intrinsics; WASM perft via node rust/bench/wasm-perft.mjs --deep --trials 3 (Node 25.7.0, Bun 1.3.10)
hardware: Apple M4 Max (arm64, macOS 26.4.1), single-threaded, min of N trials
tradeoffs: WASM path reaches only 0.40x (Node) to 0.70x (Bun) of native Rust speed; 45 KB brotli WASM plus about 10 KB TypeScript shim; async Chess.create() initialisation; no SIMD movegen because std::simd is not portable to WASM.
caveats: The chess.js and chessops figures are cited from upstream (chess.js on Node 22, other hardware) and were not run in the same harness on the M4 Max, so the 55x/95x ratios are cross-run comparisons; the code of the ultrachess side is public and reproducible with 'just bench'. Perft is a movegen microbenchmark and says nothing about full-library workloads such as PGN parsing. Young repo (43 commits, all in April 2026).
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' (ultrachess: 'Ultra-fast WASM-first chess library'), then the GitHub README and BENCH.md

name: delaunay32-wasm (Delaunay32 C++ core compiled with Emscripten)
language: C++17 compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, TypeScript API
workload: Unconstrained 2D Delaunay triangulation of 1,000,000 random points, single thread, relative runtime
claimed_speedup: Delaunay32 WASM 1.00x vs Delaunator JavaScript 5.1.0 3.71x runtime (about 3.7x faster); native Delaunay32 C++ 0.81x single-thread and 0.26x with 8 threads
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten 6.0.6 with exceptions, LTO, memory growth, no virtual filesystem and no pthreads; optimisation level not stated
tradeoffs: About 246 KB WASM (99 KB gzip); 2 GiB maximum WASM32 memory so browser limits are lower than native; targets current Chrome, Firefox and Safari with module workers, Node.js is not an official target; exact predicates only for signed 32-bit integer coordinates (floats are quantised, with a QuantizationReport).
caveats: One-line README table, not an artifact: the benchmark script for the WASM-versus-Delaunator row is not in the wasm repo (the C++ core repo morishuz/delaunay32 has delaunay_benchmark), the JavaScript runtime is not named, and runs/warmup are not stated. Relative runtime only, no absolute milliseconds. Wraps the Delaunay32 C++ library, which is already catalogued (this entry is the WASM artifact and its Delaunator-in-JS claim).
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' (delaunay32: 'Fast, exact 2D Delaunay triangulation'), then the GitHub README of morishuz/delaunay32-wasm

name: berith (Ed25519 and X25519 in Rust WebAssembly)
language: Rust (ed25519-dalek and x25519-dalek compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack) with TypeScript
workload: Ed25519 operation per iteration (deno bench and a Node bench harness) comparing berith, @noble/curves 0.7.0, supercop.wasm 5.0.1 and node:crypto
claimed_speedup: Deno 1.30.3: berith unserialized 325.78 us/iter vs @noble/curves 0.7.0 1.9 ms/iter (5.85x faster); Node 18.12.1: 281.68 us vs 1.99 ms (7.06x faster). Counter-rows on the same page: supercop.wasm 5.0.1 187.96 us/iter and node:crypto unserialized 152.67 us/iter are faster than berith
compiler_and_flags: rust 1.71.0 (Dockerfile), wasm-pack build --release; Cargo profile release opt-level 3, lto true; ed25519-dalek 2.0.0; Deno 1.30.3 and Node v18.12.1
tradeoffs: README marks the package DEPRECATED in favour of @hazae41/ed25519 and @hazae41/x25519; wasm must be initialised asynchronously (Berith.initBundledOnce); Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant; inputs and outputs cross the JS-wasm boundary and the 'serialized' variant is about 13% slower.
caveats: Baseline is @noble/curves 0.7.0 (2023); current noble releases are faster, so the 5.9-7.1x ratio is dated. The same table shows berith 1.5x slower than supercop.wasm and about 1.8x slower than node:crypto, so the win is only against pure JS. The README lists a 1.13x ratio between its own variants and mislabels slower rows as 'x faster' (0.67x, 0.54x). Output was pasted into the README; whether it was regenerated after the last commits is not stated.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript', then the GitHub README of hazae41/berith

name: markdown_yo (Yo-language Markdown renderer, WASM build)
language: Yo (new systems language) compiled to WebAssembly via Emscripten and to native
workload: Markdown-to-HTML conversion of generated inputs from 64 KB to 20 MB, median of 10 runs after 3 warmups, WASM called with --repeat 20 to amortise module startup
claimed_speedup: WASM vs markdown-it: 64 KB 12.9 vs 1.6 ms (0.1x, slower), 256 KB 13.1 vs 6.7 ms (0.5x), 1 MB 13.5 vs 28.8 ms (2.1x), 5 MB 32.6 vs 158.9 ms (4.9x), 20 MB 121.5 vs 722.8 ms (6.0x); native build 4.5x to 7.6x
compiler_and_flags: WASM: Emscripten -O3 -flto from the Yo compiler (version pinned in .yo-version), Node.js (version not stated); native: clang -O3 -flto; harness benchmark/run.js
tradeoffs: WASM module is 383 KB and has about 12 ms Node.js compile startup, so it loses to markdown-it below roughly 1 MB; 98.7% CommonMark spec pass (815/826), not full parity with markdown-it plugins; written in the young Yo language, so building needs the Yo toolchain.
caveats: The license is declared as MIT only in npm/package.json (no LICENSE file in the repo). Benchmark inputs are synthetic samples in benchmark/samples, not real documents; Node.js and Emscripten versions are not stated. Project is one month old (116 commits, version 0.0.16) and AI-assisted planning files are checked in (AGENTS.md, PLAN.md). Its 'WASM' speedups need --repeat 20 in the harness to amortise startup, which flatters single-shot use. The ratio rows of 0.1x and 0.5x are slowdowns.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' (markdown_yo), then the GitHub README and benchmark/run.js

name: cjs-module-lexer (C lexer compiled to WebAssembly)
language: C compiled to WebAssembly (wasi-sdk and Binaryen), with a JavaScript build
baseline: the same lexer's pure JavaScript build (lexer.js) running in V8/Node.js
workload: Lexing 3,635 KiB of real-world JavaScript samples (angular, d3, magic-string, rollup and their minified forms) to detect CommonJS named exports: cold run over all samples and warm runs averaged over 25
claimed_speedup: Cold run, all samples: JS build 299 ms vs Wasm build 43 ms (6.95x, derived from page data); warm run, all samples: 40.28 ms vs 27.76 ms (1.45x, README says about 1.5x faster); angular.js warm 13.96 vs 9.32 ms; module load time 4 ms (JS) vs 10 ms (Wasm)
compiler_and_flags: wasi-sdk (pinned) plus Binaryen optimisation passes, built with make (npm run build-wasm); Node version and clang flags not stated in the README
stars_or_usage: 262 stars; used by Node.js ESM-CommonJS interop
tradeoffs: Wasm build needs initSync() or await init() (ESM only; browsers should await init()); wasm instantiation adds about 6 ms of module load; detection patterns are frozen by design; both builds are lexers, not parsers, so the work per byte is small.
caveats: First-party README numbers with no CPU or Node version; run with 'npm run bench' (bench/ folder is public). Baseline is the project's own JavaScript build rather than a third-party package, and the warm-run advantage is only 1.45x; the 6.95x cold-run gap reflects JIT warm-up of the JS build that the Wasm build skips.
found_via: npm registry search 'wasm faster than javascript' results scanned for speed claims, then the GitHub README of nodejs/cjs-module-lexer (Benchmarks section)

name: md4w (md4c compiled to WebAssembly) - third-party row in the Ox Content Markdown benchmark
language: Zig and C (md4c) compiled to WebAssembly, JavaScript wrapper
workload: Markdown parse only and parse plus HTML render of a 48.7 KB document and of a roughly 1 MB document, median of 7 runs in a CI sweep dated 2026-09-25, run on Node v26.8.1
claimed_speedup: Parse + render 48.7 KB: md4w 2,361 ops/s (0.42 ms) vs markdown-it 293 ops/s (3.42 ms), 8.1x (derived from page data); parse + render ~1 MB: 116 vs 10 ops/s (8.64 ms vs 102.62 ms, 11.6x derived from page data); parse only 48.7 KB: 1,071 vs 325 ops/s (3.3x derived); parse only ~1 MB: 50 vs 11 ops/s (4.5x derived); md4w CommonMark conformance in the same table is 91.7% against 100% for markdown-it
compiler_and_flags: md4w's published prebuilt wasm (build flags of that wasm not stated); harness tools/benchmarks/bundle-size/parse-benchmark.mjs, 'vp run bench:docs' with OX_CONTENT_BENCHMARK_RUNS=7; Node v26.8.1, Bun 1.3.14
hardware: AMD EPYC, 32 logical cores (CI runner blacksmith-32vcpu-ubuntu-2404; exact model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 155 stars (md4w); the benchmark host ubugeeei-prod/ox-content has 250 stars
tradeoffs: md4w passes 91.7% of the 652 CommonMark 0.31.2 examples in the same suite, versus 100% for markdown-it, so part of the speed comes from lower spec coverage; wasm instantiation cost is not part of the ops/sec rows.
caveats: Evidence for a catalogued project, taken from the README of a competing Rust Markdown engine (Ox Content, which benchmarks itself and a source fork called Ferromark in the same tables), so the host has a stake in the ranking even though the md4w row is unmodified. md4w's own README claims only about 2.5x faster than markdown-it, so the third-party ratios (3.3x to 11.6x) are larger than the first-party claim. CPU is 'AMD EPYC' with no model number and the md4w wasm build flags are not stated, hence B rather than A. last_commit is md4w's (2025-05-28), not the benchmark host's.
found_via: npm registry crawl for wasm packages, then the Performance section of ubugeeei-prod/ox-content README

name: tape-sha256 (spool-labs/sha256) WebAssembly SIMD build
language: Rust (WebAssembly simd128 backend, also native AVX-512, AVX2, SHA-NI, NEON)
baseline: @noble/hashes SHA-256 (pure JavaScript, what @solana/web3.js 1.x uses) in V8
workload: Merkle-style batch of 64 separate ~1 KB messages hashed per call in Node (JS-to-wasm copies included), and a Chrome vanity-address grinding loop over 2048 candidates of 87 bytes
claimed_speedup: Node v24, 64-leaf batch: tape wasm 100.61 us/batch (673 MB/s) vs noble one-shot 337.97 us/batch (200 MB/s), about 3.4x (derived from page data), vs hash-wasm 156.24 us (1.55x derived). Chrome 150 grinding: 4.55 M candidates/s, 3.72x the noble/web3.js stack (1.22 M/s) and 1.61x hash-wasm (2.82 M/s)
compiler_and_flags: RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+simd128' cargo build --release --example wasm_lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown; rustc version not stated; Node v24 (V8) and Chrome 150; harnesses bench.mjs, pda.mjs, matrix.cjs and a browser/ page are in benches/wasm
stars_or_usage: 1 star; 13 commits (July-August 2026); crate tape-sha256 on crates.io
tradeoffs: Without the simd128 flag the wasm falls back to a portable-8 backend that roughly ties hash-wasm; wasm SIMD cannot reach the SHA hardware units, so Node's native crypto (42.89 us/batch) and Chrome's WebCrypto are faster for ~1 KB batches; Node results are 'unpinned, read as ratios'.
caveats: The same page states that in a browser WebCrypto beats this wasm on batched ~1 KB messages (75 us vs 80-90 us) and recommends WebCrypto there; the win is against pure-JS noble and against hash-wasm, and for small messages in synchronous loops. PDA derivation gains only 4% because the curve check dominates. Chrome clamps performance.now to 100 us, so batch rows are quantised to 5 us steps. Very young repo, single author.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly module faster than pure JS implementation benchmark table README' (github.com), page spool-labs/sha256 benches/wasm/README.md

name: md5-wasm (hand-written WebAssembly MD5)
language: WebAssembly text format (.wat) with JavaScript wrapper
baseline: md5 npm package (pure JavaScript MD5, 'the most popular md5 utility')
workload: MD5 of files from 0.2 MB to 37 MB on a low-powered Ubuntu production server with NodeJS v10.18.1, elapsed ms and MB/s per size
claimed_speedup: README: 30x faster than the most popular md5 utility. Table: 37 MB file 38,500 ms (md5) vs 990 ms (MD5-WASM), 37 MB/s vs 0.96 MB/s, about 39x (derived from page data, README says 30x); 1 MB 1,000 ms vs 170 ms; 4 MB 4,000 vs 330 ms; 0.2 MB 260 vs 90 ms; 0.5 MB 520 vs 360 ms
compiler_and_flags: hand-written WAT (four-logics-syntax.wat) assembled to wasm; NodeJS v10.18.1 on Ubuntu; no benchmark script found in the visible file list

The README expected 3-5x and attributes the larger gap to number-format conversions in the JS md5 package; the baseline md5 package is slow (about 1 MB/s) and is not a tuned JavaScript MD5, which likely inflates the ratio. Gap is 1.4x at 0.5 MB where startup dominates. Last commit message is 'Fighting with git'.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly module faster than pure JS implementation benchmark table README npm package wasm' (github.com): briantbutton/md5-wasm

name: wasm-runtime-performance (boost::graph Floyd-Warshall via Emscripten)
language: C++ (Boost.Graph, std::priority_queue) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten
baseline: graphlib.js alg.floydWarshall (JavaScript, in the browser JS engine)
workload: Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest paths on a graph with 100 vertices and 500 edges, JS graphlib vs boost::graph compiled to wasm; second test: 300,000 priority-queue inserts and peek+pop against FastPriorityQueue.js and Heap.js
claimed_speedup: With emcc -O3: JS 61.1135 ms vs WASM 10.1569 ms (about 6.0x faster, derived from page data); unoptimised wasm: 62.16 ms JS vs 1235.41 ms WASM (20x slower). README conclusion on the heap test: WASM std::priority_queue inserts 58.4 ms vs FastPriorityQueue.js 9.86 ms and Heap.js 13.42 ms (wasm 4-6x slower on inserts)
compiler_and_flags: emsdk (version not stated) with boost; unoptimised and -O3 builds via generate_output.sh; exact emcc flags not shown
tradeoffs: Needs boost and emsdk to rebuild; wasm in 2017-era browsers; wasm module startup excluded (the README says it only times execution after loading).
caveats: 2017 repo (10 commits, April-May 2017), single run outputs pasted into the README, no CPU or browser version, no licence file. Mixed result by design: the Floyd-Warshall win only appears at -O3, and the priority-queue test shows wasm slower than JS. Interesting mainly as a documented -O0 versus -O3 Emscripten difference of three orders of magnitude.

name: webgpu-shaders-study (AssemblyScript SIMD particle loop vs JavaScript)
language: AssemblyScript (WebAssembly SIMD), Rust (WebAssembly SIMD), JavaScript, WGSL
baseline: plain JavaScript loop on the CPU in the browser (V8 assumed, browser not stated)
workload: Particle simulation pulled toward the mouse, Heavy mode (16 attractors per particle), frames per second at 1M, 4M and 16M particles, same data copied to the GPU every frame in the JS and wasm demos
claimed_speedup: Heavy mode on an Apple Silicon Mac: JavaScript 33 fps at 1M and 8 fps at 4M (no 16M figure); WASM AssemblyScript 40, 37 and 6 fps (about 1.2x at 1M and 4.6x at 4M, derived from page data); WASM Rust 60, 41 and 11 fps; WebGPU 60, 60 and ~48 fps. README: Rust's step is about 15% faster than AssemblyScript's in Light mode, more in Heavy
compiler_and_flags: AssemblyScript source 2-wasm/assembly/index.ts built with 'npm run build:as' (asc flags not shown); Rust built with .cargo/config.toml simd enabled; compiled .wasm files are checked in
hardware: Apple Silicon Mac (chip model not stated)

caveats: One-commit repository with a results table pasted into the README and no licence file; fps readings are frame rates (capped at 60) not controlled timings, with a drawing and upload cost shared by all CPU variants; browser, chip model and asc version are not stated; the JS 16M cell is blank. Counter-evidence from the same table: at 1M particles the AssemblyScript build is only 1.2x the JS loop. The code is public (index.html overview and demos) but there is no benchmark harness.
found_via: WebSearch 'AssemblyScript benchmark faster than JavaScript SIMD implementation speedup' (github.com): anshullaikar/webgpu-shaders-study
